sections.title: Why a single cell can rely on diffusion
paragraphs: A small unicellular organism has a large surface area compared with its volume. Much of its material lies close to the surrounding water, so substances have only a short distance to travel between the surface and the cell interior.

Oxygen can diffuse into an aerobic cell when its concentration is higher outside. Respiration uses oxygen inside and releases carbon dioxide, helping maintain gradients for oxygen entry and carbon dioxide loss. Diffusion is net movement down a concentration gradient; particles still move in both directions.

This explains why simple unicellular organisms can depend on diffusion for exchange with their surroundings. It does not mean that every substance crosses every cell membrane freely or that cells never use active transport.

example.question: Compare cubes of side 1 mm and 4 mm as models of cell size.
steps: For side s, surface area = 6s² and volume = s³; surface area per volume = 6/s.
The 1 mm cube has 6 mm²/mm³; the 4 mm cube has 1.5 mm²/mm³.
The larger cube has more total surface but less surface per volume, and a longer distance from its surface to its centre.
example.explanation: Exchange capacity must be compared with demand, distance and the maintained gradient.

practice.question: Does a larger total surface alone prove that a cell exchanges substances more effectively?
practice.answer: No. Compare surface with the volume needing supply and consider diffusion distance and gradients.
practice.explanation: Exchange capacity must be compared with demand, distance and the maintained gradient.

commonMistakes: Do not confuse total surface area with surface area per volume.
Diffusion does not stop all molecular movement at equilibrium.

sections.title: Why larger organisms need internal transport
paragraphs: A large multicellular organism contains cells far from its outside surface. Its outer surface is relatively small compared with its volume, while many cells need nutrients and may need oxygen and waste removal.

Diffusion over a long distance is too slow to meet these demands. Specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems carry substances between distant parts: blood circulation in humans, and xylem and phloem in flowering plants.

Transport over a long distance and diffusion across a short distance work together. Blood flow brings oxygen near body cells, then oxygen diffuses from capillary blood to the cells. A transport system does not eliminate the need for diffusion.

example.question: Why does blood flow not make capillary walls unnecessary?
steps: Flow carries blood over the long route from the lungs to tissues.
The thin capillary wall provides a short final diffusion distance.
Both delivery by flow and local exchange are needed.
example.explanation: Link the size problem to a delivery route and a short local exchange step.

practice.question: Why is diffusion directly from the skin insufficient for all cells deep inside a human?
practice.answer: The distances are too long and the outer surface is too small relative to the demand of the body volume.
practice.explanation: Link the size problem to a delivery route and a short local exchange step.

commonMistakes: Do not say diffusion is absent from large organisms.

sections.title: Follow sucrose and amino acids in phloem
paragraphs: Phloem carries dissolved sucrose and amino acids between leaves and other parts of a plant. Movement of these organic solutes is called translocation. A photosynthesising mature leaf commonly supplies sucrose to growing or storage tissues.

A source supplies solute; a sink receives it for use or storage. Roots, developing fruits and growing shoots can act as sinks. Stored material may later supply new growth, so a storage organ can become a source at a different time.
Movement can be upwards or downwards in different phloem pathways, depending on the source and sink. Phloem is not defined as a permanently downward route, and it does not carry only sucrose.

example.question: A mature leaf supplies sucrose to a developing fruit above it and a root below it. Is one route impossible?
steps: The leaf is the source and both receiving organs are sinks.
Different phloem pathways can carry solutes towards the different sinks.
Direction depends on the source–sink arrangement, not simply on height.
example.explanation: Identify the transported material and the supplying and receiving tissues.

practice.question: Name the two organic substances specified for phloem transport.
practice.explanation: Identify the transported material and the supplying and receiving tissues.

commonMistakes: Do not restrict phloem to downward transport or call glucose its only cargo.

sections.title: Follow water and mineral ions in xylem
paragraphs: Xylem transports water and dissolved mineral ions from the roots to the stem, leaves and other parts of a plant. These ions include substances needed to make new biological molecules; they are not sucrose transported from a leaf.

Xylem vessels form continuous tubes. Mature conducting vessel elements have lost their living contents, and their lignified walls support the plant and resist collapse while water is pulled through them.

Water loss from leaves helps maintain the transpiration stream. Water molecules cohere to one another, allowing tension to be transmitted along a water column. The plant does not contain a heart pumping water from its roots.

example.question: A root absorbs nitrate ions and a leaf makes sucrose. Choose the long-distance transport tissue for each.
steps: Water carrying nitrate ions from the roots travels in xylem.
Sucrose moving from a source leaf to a sink travels in phloem.
The tissues differ in their cargo and function.
example.explanation: Keep the xylem water-and-mineral route separate from organic-solute translocation.

practice.question: Are mineral ions transported from roots to leaves by phloem in the specified pathway?
practice.answer: No. That water-and-mineral-ion pathway is xylem.
practice.explanation: Keep the xylem water-and-mineral route separate from organic-solute translocation.

commonMistakes: Do not describe conducting xylem vessels as living cells that actively pump water.

sections.title: Explain water entry into root hairs
paragraphs: A root hair is an extension of a root epidermal cell. Its long, narrow shape provides a large area in contact with water between soil particles.

When soil water has a higher water potential than the root hair cell contents, water enters the cell by osmosis through its partially permeable cell membrane. Dissolved substances in the cell lower its water potential. The cell wall is not the partially permeable membrane responsible for osmosis.

Water passes across root tissues towards xylem and is carried onwards. Mineral-ion uptake is a separate process: ions are not absorbed by osmosis, and active transport may be needed when uptake is against their concentration gradient.
The direction depends on the gradient. Very dry or salty soil can have a low water potential, so water entry is reduced or water may leave cells. Do not assume that every root always gains water.

example.question: Soil water has water potential −0.10 MPa and a root hair has −0.40 MPa. Predict net water movement.
steps: −0.10 MPa is the higher water potential: it is less negative.
Water moves from soil into the root hair down the water-potential gradient.
This is osmosis across the partially permeable cell membrane.
example.explanation: State both the membrane and the direction of the water-potential gradient.

practice.question: Would water enter the same cell from soil water at −0.60 MPa?
practice.answer: Not down that gradient. The soil water potential is lower than the cell value, so the net direction would be out of the cell.
practice.explanation: State both the membrane and the direction of the water-potential gradient.

commonMistakes: Do not call mineral-ion uptake osmosis.
A more negative water potential is lower, not higher.

sections.title: Trace water loss from a leaf
paragraphs: Transpiration is water loss by evaporation from plant surfaces. In a typical leaf, water evaporates from moist mesophyll cell walls into the air spaces; water vapour then diffuses through stomata into the outside air.

Evaporation is the change from liquid water to vapour. Diffusion carries that vapour down its concentration gradient. These are connected steps, but evaporation and diffusion do not mean the same thing.

Water lost from the leaf is replaced by water from xylem. This contributes to the transpiration stream from roots to shoots. The stomata are pores, controlled by guard cells, rather than tiny pumps that push water out.

Most loss in many leaves is through stomata, but plant surfaces can also lose water through other routes such as the cuticle. The specification definition is not restricted to liquid water droplets falling from a leaf.

example.question: Put xylem, mesophyll cell walls, leaf air spaces and outside air in the water-loss route.
steps: Xylem supplies water to leaf tissues.
Water evaporates from moist mesophyll walls into leaf air spaces.
Water vapour diffuses through stomata into outside air.
example.explanation: Follow water through its liquid-to-vapour change and then its diffusion route.

practice.question: Is transpiration the same as respiration?
practice.answer: No. Transpiration is evaporative water loss; respiration transfers energy from organic molecules.
practice.explanation: Follow water through its liquid-to-vapour change and then its diffusion route.

commonMistakes: Do not describe evaporation as movement of liquid water through an open pore.
Transpiration and translocation are different processes.

sections.title: Explain humidity and air movement
paragraphs: For comparable leaves with similar stomatal opening and temperature, humid outside air contains more water vapour. This reduces the gradient between moist leaf air spaces and the outside air, so transpiration generally falls.

Moving air removes water vapour accumulating close to a leaf. This reduces the humid boundary layer and maintains a steeper gradient, so increasing wind speed generally raises transpiration if the plant remains adequately supplied with water.

These are conditional comparisons, not universal straight-line laws. Severe drying can lead to stomatal closure, reducing loss; wind may also change leaf temperature. A controlled investigation must separate the chosen factor from these other changes.

example.question: Two equally lit shoots are at the same temperature. One is surrounded by humid air. Explain its lower water-loss rate.
steps: The humid air has a higher water-vapour concentration.
The gradient from the leaf air spaces to the outside air is smaller.
Net outward vapour diffusion is slower, provided other conditions and stomatal opening are comparable.
example.explanation: Explain each condition through the vapour gradient at the leaf surface.

practice.question: Why can a fan increase water loss without changing the number of leaves?
practice.answer: It removes humid air near the leaf and helps maintain the outward water-vapour gradient.
practice.explanation: Explain each condition through the vapour gradient at the leaf surface.

commonMistakes: Do not explain higher humidity as increasing the outward gradient.
Wind does not need to create more stomata to affect the rate.

sections.title: Explain light and temperature effects
paragraphs: With other conditions comparable, a rise in temperature usually increases evaporation and water-vapour movement, raising transpiration while water remains available and stomata remain open.

In many plants, increasing light causes stomata to open for carbon dioxide uptake during photosynthesis. The wider openings also allow more water-vapour loss. This is a stomatal effect; light is not itself a substance being transported through the leaf.
A lamp can change both light intensity and leaf temperature. A valid light comparison measures or limits the warming effect rather than assuming that moving the lamp changes only light.

Stomatal behaviour differs with species and water stress. Darkness often reduces stomatal loss, but total water loss need not become exactly zero. Avoid extrapolating that transpiration always rises indefinitely with temperature or light.

example.question: A closer lamp increases bubble movement in a potometer. Does this establish a light effect alone?
steps: The lamp may also warm the leaf and surrounding air.
Measure temperature and keep it comparable, for example using a cooler light source and a suitable heat-control arrangement.
Only then can the change be attributed more securely to the light treatment.
example.explanation: Distinguish the mechanism of a factor from unintended changes in the same experiment.

practice.question: Why may brighter light increase transpiration in a well-watered plant?
practice.answer: Stomata often open more for carbon dioxide uptake, allowing more water vapour to escape.
practice.explanation: Distinguish the mechanism of a factor from unintended changes in the same experiment.

commonMistakes: Do not claim zero transpiration in every plant in darkness.
Do not ignore lamp heating when investigating light.

sections.title: Set up a bubble potometer
paragraphs: A bubble potometer follows water uptake by a cut leafy shoot. Water drawn into the shoot moves a deliberately introduced air bubble along a narrow, water-filled tube. The bubble is a visible marker; it is not the water being absorbed.

The connections and shoot seal must be watertight and airtight. Prepare the shoot and connect it under water to reduce air entering and interrupting the xylem water column. Use a healthy leafy shoot and allow it to settle in the test conditions before timing.

Begin with water-filled apparatus and no unwanted air pockets. Introduce one small marker bubble by the apparatus-specific method, then keep the capillary inlet in water. A reservoir and valve, if fitted, can reset the marker between readings; close the reset valve during timing.

Read the same edge of the marker against a scale at the start and end of a known time interval. Water uptake pulls the marker towards the shoot. This investigation uses a cut shoot, so it does not directly measure root-hair absorption.

example.question: A bubble moves towards the shoot during a trial. What is the quantity being followed?
steps: The shoot draws water through the capillary.
The marker position changes as water is taken up.
Movement per time estimates uptake rate; it is not a direct mass measurement of evaporated water.
example.explanation: Keep one defined water route and one visible marker during the timed interval.

practice.question: Should the reservoir reset valve remain open during the timed reading?
practice.answer: No. The reservoir could supply water along another route and invalidate the capillary reading.
practice.explanation: Keep one defined water route and one visible marker during the timed interval.

commonMistakes: Do not allow leaks or unwanted air pockets and still treat the result as reliable.
Do not describe this cut-shoot apparatus as a direct root-uptake test.

diagram.alt: Original schematic of a leafy shoot sealed to a water-filled capillary, with one marker bubble moving towards the shoot, a closed reservoir reset valve and the inlet below water.
diagram.caption: Original bubble-potometer model, not to scale. The closed valve keeps the reservoir out of the timed route; the marker moves towards the shoot.

sections.title: Calculate water uptake from bubble movement
paragraphs: In the same capillary, compare distance moved divided by elapsed time. State units such as mm/min. Distance rate alone is not a volume rate; capillary width matters when comparing different tubes.
If the internal radius r is known, the water volume represented by marker displacement d is πr²d. Use matching length units and the internal radius, not the outer tube radius or the diameter.

Divide this volume by time for uptake per time. Because 1 cm³ = 1,000 mm³, a rate in mm³/min is divided by 1,000 to express it in cm³/min. These calculated rates are uptake proxies, not exact transpiration measurements.
All numbers below are constructed teaching examples, not observations from a trial. Give a sensible precision and retain unrounded values while calculating.

example.question: A capillary of internal radius 0.50 mm has a marker displacement of 24 mm in 3.0 min. Calculate the uptake rate.
steps: Distance rate = 24 ÷ 3.0 = 8.0 mm/min.
Cross-sectional area = π × (0.50)² ≈ 0.7854 mm².
Volume moved ≈ 0.7854 × 24 = 18.85 mm³.
Uptake rate ≈ 18.85 ÷ 3.0 = 6.3 mm³/min, or 0.0063 cm³/min to two significant figures.
example.explanation: Check what is measured, convert it into volume when justified, and preserve the units.

practice.question: A second tube has twice the internal radius and the same distance per minute. Does it indicate the same volume uptake?
practice.answer: No. Cross-sectional area is four times greater, so the volume rate is four times greater.
practice.explanation: Check what is measured, convert it into volume when justified, and preserve the units.

commonMistakes: Do not treat mm/min as cm³/min.
Using the diameter as the radius makes the area four times too large.

sections.title: Investigate one environmental factor
paragraphs: Choose one independent variable, such as air speed at the shoot, and measure the resulting water-uptake rate. Keep the shoot, leaf area, capillary, timed interval, light, temperature and humidity comparable unless one of those is the chosen factor.

For a wind investigation, compare still air with several measured air speeds from a fan. Distance from the fan can define a treatment, but it is not a direct measurement of air speed. Check that the fan does not unintentionally change temperature.

Allow a consistent settling period after each change. Reset the marker, repeat readings and calculate the mean of rates. Vary or alternate the treatment order and repeat a baseline to detect drift as the cut shoot changes. Repeated readings of one shoot are not independent plant replicates.

Other investigations can vary measured humidity, temperature or light while controlling the remaining conditions. Enclosing a shoot may change humidity, temperature and light together; a lamp can heat it. State how these confounders will be checked.

Use units in a results table and plot uptake rate against a measured continuous factor, or compare defined treatment groups appropriately. Conclude only what the data support for the tested shoots and conditions.

example.question: Constructed rates from one treatment are 7, 8 and 9 mm/min; a comparable treatment gives 11, 12 and 13 mm/min. Compare them.
steps: The means are 8 and 12 mm/min; the spread of repeated values should also be considered.
Percentage increase = (12 − 8) ÷ 8 × 100 = 50%.
This illustrates calculation only. Three repeated readings are not proof of a universal effect or three independent shoots.
example.explanation: A useful investigation defines the treatment, keeps comparisons fair and reports uncertainty.

practice.question: If a humidity enclosure also warms the shoot, what weakens the conclusion?
practice.answer: Humidity and temperature both changed, so the effect cannot be attributed to humidity alone without further controls.
practice.explanation: A useful investigation defines the treatment, keeps comparisons fair and reports uncertainty.

commonMistakes: Do not change several conditions and attribute the result to one.
Do not invent collected data or count repeated readings as independent plants.

apparatus: Healthy leafy shoot; teacher-prepared bubble potometer and water
Fan and air-speed meter for a wind comparison
method: Check seals, exclude unwanted air and introduce one marker.
Record a baseline after a consistent settling period.
Apply one defined treatment and recheck controlled conditions.
Measure one bubble edge displacement over a known interval with the reset valve closed.
Reset, repeat and vary the order; repeat the baseline.
Calculate rates and means; compare spread and percentage change when the baseline is nonzero.
variables: Independent: measured air speed for the proposed wind investigation.
Controls: shoot/leaf area, capillary, time interval, light, temperature and humidity.
safety: Teacher or technician prepares cut shoots and glass connections; avoid sharp edges.
Use a stable stand and manage spills.
Keep electrical fans and lights away from water and follow the school risk assessment.
quality: Use a visible displacement and read at eye level against the scale.
Allow equilibration, investigate leaks and avoid unwanted air pockets.
Do not remove selected inconvenient readings without a stated reason.
Compare independent shoots with leaf area considered; keep within-shoot repeats distinct.

sections.title: Evaluate what the potometer actually measures
paragraphs: A bubble potometer measures uptake into the cut shoot. Some absorbed water can be retained for growth, maintain cell water content or participate in metabolism, so uptake is not necessarily identical to evaporative loss.

In steady conditions, uptake can be a useful estimate of transpiration. During a sudden change, water stored in the shoot may be lost or replenished, so short-term uptake and loss can differ. Do not assume a fixed percentage is transpired in every trial.

A leak, trapped air, unequal capillary widths, changing leaf area or reading errors can distort comparisons. Repeats help reveal variation, but repeating a leaking setup does not remove its systematic error.

A suitable mass-loss investigation can provide a more direct estimate of water leaving a plant or apparatus if evaporation from exposed water and soil is prevented or separately controlled. It has its own limitations; it is not automatically a perfect reference.

example.question: A student says: “Every millimetre of bubble movement proves the exact amount of water evaporated.” Evaluate the claim.
steps: Millimetres measure marker displacement, not volume unless capillary area is known.
Even calculated volume is water uptake into the shoot.
Stored water, growth and metabolic uses prevent assuming exact equality with evaporation.
Steady conditions and a sound setup can still make uptake a useful proxy.
example.explanation: Separate the measured quantity, the inferred process and the assumptions linking them.

practice.question: Will averaging many readings automatically correct an unnoticed leak?
practice.answer: No. A leak can bias every reading; repair the apparatus and repeat the comparison.
practice.explanation: Separate the measured quantity, the inferred process and the assumptions linking them.

commonMistakes: Do not assert a universal fixed uptake-to-loss percentage.
Do not equate repeated readings with freedom from systematic error.
